A sustained fall in fertility is a relatively recent phenomenon. Before the late 18th century, two large agrarian civilisations constrained population growth by mechanisms additional to natural mortality. In western Europe delayed marriage of women, and, even more effective, forgone marriage, kept down the birth rate, as individuals strove to ensure that families would not begin their existence doomed to poverty.1–3 In China, Japan, and some North Indian castes the family was protected from starvation and penury by infanticide, predominantly of girls, which was greatest during subsistence crises (Zhao Z. Australian Population Association conference, Adelaide, 1996).

From the late 18th century a sustained fall in fertility began in France, and fertility declines became general in western and central Europe, as well as in English speaking settlement countries, in the last quarter of the 19th century.4 The reasons were complex. The fall in mortality—itself the product of social and behavioural change as well as scientific and technological advance—made a fall in fertility possible and ultimately inevitable. In France, with the revolution forcing the church into retreat and leading to a rethinking of social values and personal relationships, the fall started a century before that in richer Britain. In Britain there was a sustained and effective battle, led by the medical profession, to preserve the Victorian spousal relationship from the morally corruptive impact of the discussion and practice of contraception.5

The introduction of child labour laws and then compulsory schooling, devised with other aims, hastened the control of family size by increasing spending on children and reducing their earning potential. Control of fertility was aided in Britain and other English speaking countries by the debate over the 1877 trial of Bradlaugh and Besant for their republication of a family planning manual. The trial was reported in the new popular press and read about by the greatly expanded literate classes.6 The fact that the press mentioned contraception at all, even though almost always adversely, provided information and some legitimacy. A stronger demand for contraception led to its greater availability in a more usable form. Most of these elements in the first fertility transition were to be present in its global extension.

## Summary points

Demographic, economic, social, and administrative changes have all had a role in fertility transition

Fertility decline has never been an unconscious social process; advocacy and organisation have been important

The fertility transition has been a single global event and is an aspect of the creation of a global economy and society

Better contraception had a significant role after 1960 in developing and developed countries

The transition is far from over among large parts of the world’s population, especially south Asia and sub-Saharan Africa

Stationary global population in the next century will probably be followed by a fall in population

## Methods

This article is drawn from 40 years of experience with the Third World fertility transition, most of the field work being carried out in Asia and sub-Saharan Africa in collaboration with Pat Caldwell and demographers from these regions. The research has been published in demographic journals, and the generalisations and theoretical constructions built on them are reported here. Earlier work of this type was focused on sub-Saharan Africa,7 India,8 a comparison between the experience of Asia and Africa,9 and the global experience.10 During the last few years, primarily with Rockefeller Foundation funding, I have been developing global theory further with a strong historical element.4,11–13 This endeavour has been greatly helped by the European Fertility Project carried out by Princeton University’s Office of Population Research in the 1960s and 1970s14 and by the reconstruction of the demographic experience of all countries since 1950 undertaken by the United Nations Population Division and published in their continuing series of population projections.15

## Global society

The transition in fertility began in the early years of this century in southern and eastern Europe, Argentina, and Uruguay and during the 1920s in Japan. But it was not until the early 1940s that it began to be argued that eventually the transition would embrace the whole world, an argument based at that time on the precedents set by only Russia and Japan.16 It was felt, doubtless correctly at the time, that mortality and income levels in Asia, Africa, and tropical South America precluded such a change. But these conditions altered earlier and faster than anyone had forecast.

Almost immediately after the second world war mortality began to fall steeply in much of Asia and Latin America and somewhat more slowly in sub-Saharan Africa. In Japan and Sri Lanka 12 or more years were added to life expectancies in six or seven elapsed years. This achievement has not been completely satisfactorily explained. It was partly due to better medicines and insecticides and far better global cooperation. The accumulated public health experience in pre-war colonies helped. So did more local control and higher aspirations as independence was achieved or drew near. Rising educational levels and the reduction in the numbers of isolated subsistence farmers with the growth of the world economy were also important.

By the early 1950s there was not only an acceptance that mortality and fertility would eventually fall throughout the world but a growing conviction that the fertility decline had to be encouraged and accelerated. This movement was greatly assisted by Prime Minister Nehru’s declaration in 1951 that India would establish a national family planning programme. Gradually, during the 1950s and early 1960s national family planning programmes were established in most of south, South East, and east Asia, in parts of north Africa, and in a few Caribbean and Latin American countries. They received increasing external funding and contraceptive supplies, predominantly from the United States, supplemented by aid from northwestern Europe, American foundations, and the United Nations. Nevertheless, the model was primarily Asian and the greatest successes were in Asia. Asian countries combined the provision of contraceptives with assistance with their use, usually in the context of organised moral advocacy by government and community leaders about the family and national need for fertility control. This governmental advocacy was probably of decisive importance in large parts of Asia, where Brahminism and Confucianism provided a tradition of elite moral leadership and where there was no entrenched religion with tenets opposing contraception.

## Since 1965

For 20 years after the second world war, and a decade and a half after India proclaimed its national family planning programme, fertility in third world countries showed no sign of decline and the acceptance of contraception was modest. From 1950 to 1965 world population increased by 34% and that of developing countries by 39%.15 In developing countries, in the 15 years from the early 1950s until the late 1960s, life expectancy at birth had risen from under 41 years to over 52 years and the annual population growth rate had climbed from 2.0% to 2.5% while the total fertility rate (the average number of lifetime births per woman at the age specific birth rates at a specified date) had remained at just over six. Social theorists began to proclaim that it was unique characteristics of the Western family that had allowed or ordained fertility control, and others suggested that the socioeconomic gap between the late 19th century West and the mid-20th century Third World was greater than had been thought. But by 1970 it was clear that there had been a widespread fall in fertility from about 1965 in both Latin America and Asia.

What had caused the fall was less clear. Possibly the most important factor was a build up in the West and among the elite populations in the Third World of the view that fertility control was necessary and even virtuous and that contraception was respectable and could be publicly discussed. The media and Western universities (where the necessity for controlling fertility was increasingly an article of faith) played an important part in educating those who governed developing countries or advised those who governed. The developing world’s educational levels had risen. By 1965, over 80% of the children of the relevant age groups were in primary schools and 20% in secondary schools. Young parents were more media conscious and far more conscious of the cost of schooling. The global economy was forming, and the prospect of children getting employment in the modern sector of the economy made parents determined to keep their children in school even if the cost could be met only by limiting family size.

Other changes were taking place. The family planning programmes were gaining experience and covering more people. Furthermore, the early 1960s saw developments that made lowering fertility easier. The first modern intrauterine device, the Lippes loop, became available, and then oral contraception. Suction abortion was developed. In India and elsewhere more doctors added tubectomies to their previous skills in performing vasectomies and many were trained in laparoscopy. These were the main methods used by all the successful family planning programmes in large Third World countries.

In the three decades, 1965-70 to 1995-2000, the total fertility rate of the developing world halved from 6.0 to 3.0 births per woman.15 What has been less frequently noted is that between the early 1960s and the late 1990s the total fertility rate of developed countries fell by 37% from 2.7 to 1.7. Fertility in the West fell because married women were entering the labour force in larger numbers than before, but undoubtedly the change was facilitated by the same forces that assisted the Third World: there were better contraceptives and their use had become respectable. Thus the world’s annual number of births in the late 1990s was only 129 million, well below the 206 million which would have been the situation if the fertility levels of the early 1960s had been maintained. Two thirds of the fall in births was contributed by Asia, almost half the world’s decline by China and India alone. Most of the balance was shared between the developed world (10%), Latin America (12%), and Africa, predominantly north Africa (8%).

The Latin American fall in fertility began at about the same socioeconomic and demographic level as the fall in the West (by measures such as real income per capita, education, and infant mortality). The opposition of the Catholic church to contraception meant that Latin America had few national family planning programmes and individuals had doubts about using contraceptives. In contrast, falls in fertility in most of the larger countries of Asia (India, China, Bangladesh, and Indonesia) began at lower socioeconomic and demographic levels, at least partly because of massive national family planning programmes and the message that practising contraception was virtuous. The programmes were effective because of rising levels of education, the desire that children should be prepared for non-farming occupations, and land shortages in densely crowded and much divided farm land.
